issues.title: ADR set: correctness/staleness/cohesion pass, and an implementation-status field the website can render
issues.body:
Raised by Pip 2026-07-31, from the website side, after a honesty sweep found that the
website's published rendering of these ADRs makes claims the ADRs themselves do not
support.

## Why this is urgent-ish rather than tidy-up

`pdoom1-website` renders 17 of these ADRs to **public pages** at
`https://pdoom1.com/design-notes/`, via `scripts/sync/sync-design-notes.py`. The
generator wraps every page in framing text that reads:

> These are the actual decision records the game is built from … They describe *why*
> the game works the way it does.

That framing is **present tense and uniform**, and it is false for at least three:

- **ADR-0005** (emergent waves / seed schedules) is published as live design, but
  pdoom1#1020 states: *"ADR-0005 seed schedules are INERT in real play: nothing passes a
  schedule to GameState, so `event_schedule` is always empty."* The page even tells a
  player that *"the turn-9 funding wave on this week's seed becomes community
  vocabulary"* — a mechanic that does not fire. A league player could plan around it.
- **ADR-0003** (Liability Ledger) appears in the roadmap under *"Further out — wanted,
  not scheduled"*.
- **ADR-0007**'s own status says *build **third**, strictly after ADR-0003 and ADR-0004* —
  i.e. not built.

The website will fix its own framing. But the underlying question is yours: **which of
these records describe shipped behaviour, and which describe intent?** Nothing in the
current format distinguishes them, so no downstream consumer can either.

## What Pip is asking for

1. **A correctness / staleness / cohesion pass over the whole ADR set.** For each:
   is it accurate today, superseded, partially implemented, or aspirational?
2. **A machine-readable implementation status.** The website already renders the
   `Status:` line verbatim, so an added field — e.g. `Implemented: yes | partial | no` —
   would let the published page say `ACCEPTED — not yet implemented` automatically,
   with no website change beyond reading one field. This is the smallest fix that
   removes the whole class.
3. **Vocabulary drift.** ADR-0011 describes *"Current build: one global AP pool"* — the
   AP pool has since been removed for the attention economy (pdoom1#1037 is already
   sweeping stale AP wording). "Current build" is unambiguously present tense on a page
   dated three weeks ago. Consider a convention: never write *"current build"* in a
   record that outlives the build.
4. **Publication pipeline.** `sync-design-notes.yml` renders from the latest **release
   tag**, so ADR-0018 (on `main` since 2026-07-27) is not published and a reader cannot
   tell. That is defensible, but it is undocumented. Decide and document: do design
   notes track `main` or the last release? Then make the rendered page state which.

## Cross-repo note

`docs/PLAN_EVENT_INTEGRATION.md` still describes `historical_events.json` as
*"20 events, OLD format"* — it now holds 1,194. And `CHANGELOG.md` has no mention of
`pdoom-data`, `historical_events` or `EventService` at all, so the integration that
~2,190 published website pages describe is undocumented in the game's own changelog.
Worth folding into the same pass.

Filed from pdoom1-website so it is not lost. Happy to take any part of this on the
website side.

issues.title: ui(layout): the Plan screen wastes its middle and scatters its text -- legibility-first layout brief
issues.body:
Captured via the **F6 flight recorder** during a 2026-07-30 16:44 session, at turn 1 with a fresh state (doom 20.0, $245,000) -- so this is explicitly the **new-player opening view**, not a late-game screen. Screenshot and full `state.json` are in the capture:

`%APPDATA%\Godot\app_userdata\P(Doom)\flight_recorder\session_20260730_164411\`

Pip's note, verbatim and unedited, because it reads as a coherent brief rather than a bug list:

> "The vertical stack of buttons should be arranged such that the player doesn't need to scroll to see anything from a starting perspective. The upgrades on the right hand side need to have a vertical column to go up and down like the buttons on the left. We can try having them mirror the icon button stacks but with their vertical slice extending to the top of the screen as well, experiment with wireframing other locations, and consider what parts of the simulation we want to have persistently visible across both Plan and Watch screens, if any. If we don't want to put them on the Plan space, we should workshop UI improvements to the middle of the screen, which is wasted dead space. We can prioritise increasing legibility, particularly legibility for new players. The amount of scattered text over the screen is hard to read for older players, and more instructions should be more intuitive and we should have one more centralised location for text and not otherwise clutter the screen up too much with it. It's not obvious how to progress or end the turn, these things should be spelled out for new players explicitly within the first turn's setup / suggested setup."

## The distinct asks inside it

1. **No scrolling at the opening view.** The left button stack must fit without scrolling from a standing start.
2. **Upgrades need their own vertical column** on the right, scrollable like the left stack -- candidate treatment is mirroring the left icon stack with the vertical slice running to the top of the screen.
3. **Wireframe alternatives before committing.** Explicitly an experiment, not a chosen design.
4. **Decide what stays persistently visible across Plan and Watch.** This is a screen-architecture question, not a layout tweak, and it should be answered before (2) is built -- it changes what the columns are even for.
5. **The middle of the screen is wasted dead space.** Either it earns its area or the flanking columns should claim it. Pip flagged the same thing in the morning playtest: *"the buttons on the left-hand side of the screen I find was to have all this wasted space in the middle"* (#1041, [2:37]).
6. **Legibility first, new players first.** Scattered text across the whole screen is hard to read. Consolidate to fewer, more central text locations; stop cluttering.
7. **How to progress / end the turn is not obvious.** It should be stated explicitly in the first turn's setup or a suggested-setup flow.

## Why this is one issue rather than seven

Items 1, 2, 4 and 5 are all the same question -- what the Plan screen's columns are FOR, and therefore where they live and how wide they are. Fixing them piecemeal produces a layout that is locally better and globally incoherent. Item 4 in particular is upstream of the rest.

Items 6 and 7 are a separate axis (legibility and onboarding) but land on the same surface, so they should be designed together rather than sequentially.

## Related

- #1041 -- the morning playtest's UI findings, including the same dead-middle observation and the hiring/leaderboard screens wanting more room
- #1029 -- intro replay, needed to iterate on item 7 at all without deleting a config value by hand each time
- #814 -- progressive disclosure onboarding (operator monologue, greyed-UI intro, hire waterfall)
- #889 -- Architecture Week / `main_ui.gd` monolith, which is where a real layout rework would have to live

Not for the league. This is design work, and the note itself says "experiment" and "workshop".

## Process note

This capture is the first use of the F6 flight recorder as an actual feedback channel, and it worked exactly as intended: one keypress produced a screenshot, the full serialized game state, and a typed note, all timestamped together. Considerably better evidence than a video frame plus a transcript. Worth keeping as the standard for design observations, with recorded video reserved for things that need motion.

issues.title: art(review): generation was paid for and the outputs were never reviewed -- inventory the backlog and package a decision session
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only).

## Observation

**[10:04]** "I am also thinking now that I want to just do a big bunch of art reviewing. So I'd also just like to be reminded where that's at and then like maybe I can go make a few hundred decisions. **I think I spent a bunch of money and then like haven't actually kind of seen the outputs from it as well.** So I feel like that's also a pretty big like if we package this we can get this shipped."

The failure shape: generation spend is flowing (and policy says keep it flowing), but the REVIEW half of the loop -- Pip looking at outputs and saying yes/no -- has fallen behind, so paid-for assets sit unreviewed and unshipped. This is the choke point Pip named at [12:27] in general form: "I'm not actually constrained by effort here, I'm constrained by choice."

## Ask

1. **Inventory first**: enumerate every generated-but-unreviewed batch (gpt-image-1 runs under `art_generated/` / `tools/assets` outputs, pixellab jobs, the endgame poster batch #1024 if regenerated) with counts and dates. "Remind me where that's at" is literally the ask -- Pip does not currently know the size of the backlog, and neither does the repo.
2. **Package a decision session**: one local HTML review gallery (repo-resident, per his standing local-tools preference) covering the whole backlog, batched for a few hundred rapid verdicts in one sitting. The review-tool patterns from the 2026-07-25 waves exist; #745 (compare-and-contrast mode) and #929 (verdict provenance) are the tooling issues to lean on or extend.
3. **Then close the loop**: approved assets flow to the #951 integration lane; rejects get recorded so they are not regenerated blind.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming any specific batch is good or bad -- the point is nobody can claim that yet, because they have not been looked at.
- Not proposing new tooling beyond what #745/#929 already scope -- if the existing review flow suffices, just run it.

Related: #745 (compare-and-contrast review mode), #929 (verdict provenance), #850 (post-approval coherence/dedup pass -- runs AFTER this), #951 (integration lane), #1024 (poster batch), #934 (cycle-closeout script).

issues.title: art(sweep): events name physical things the office never shows -- install a security system, no cameras appear; sweep events for asset refs, then bulk-generate
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frames `f106_559s.jpg`, `f119_623s.jpg`).

## Observation

**[10:21]** "I'm going to install a security system. Hey, if I install a security system then the lab should get some security cameras. So let's get some security cameras as art assets and let's do a sweep of all of our in-game events for reference to assets. And then use that to generate another 50 or 100 assets now."

Frames: the "Equipment Gone Missing" event offers `[Q] Install Security System ($35,000)`. Pip took it. The office floor -- which DOES visibly react to other state (cat adoption at [8:24] "I now have an actual cat", staff sprites, server rack, water cooler) -- shows nothing for it. $35,000 spent, zero visible consequence in the world the player watches all game.

The general defect: events and upgrades NAME physical things (security system, equipment, laptops, computing clusters) that the office sim never shows. Every such reference is a pre-scoped, high-confidence asset brief going unused -- and the office has already proven the payoff pattern with the cat.

## Ask (Pip's, near-verbatim)

1. **Sweep**: walk `godot/data/` (events, actions, upgrades JSON) and extract every noun that implies a visible object or office change. Output a table: source id -> implied asset -> exists? -> office hook.
2. **Generate**: use the table to drive a bulk generation batch -- Pip sized it at "another 50 or 100 assets now" [10:39]. Spend policy is active (free to $100AUD/day until 2026-08-15). Pipelines: in-repo gpt-image-1 tooling (`tools/assets`) for icons/props, pixellab for office-floor sprites.
3. **Wire the exemplar**: security system install -> camera sprites appear in the lab. One end-to-end case proves the sweep->generate->integrate loop before the batch lands (#951 is the integration lane pattern).

## Not claimed

- Not claiming every event needs an asset -- the sweep produces the candidate list; curation is the review loop's job.
- Not claiming mechanics change -- purely visual consequence wiring.

Related: #951 (integration/closeout lane pattern), #900 (art ramp round-2 gap-fill -- this sweep is its shopping list), #925 (office W3 pre-build), #913 (office juice -- same visible-consequence family), #934 (cycle-closeout script for when the batch finishes).

issues.title: design(hiring): no hire may be onboarded-by-silence -- every hiring route must surface the choice; arrivals come through a door
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only). Design ruling stated on tape, plus a presentation ask.

## The invariant Pip stated

**[9:19]** "If I fast-track hiring someone, I need to then have their onboarding reminders pop up. The player definitely needs to be given the option to choose whether and how they onboard each new staff member. **That can't default to not happening silently, they have to choose to forget it at least once.**"

Current state: the onboarding choice window (reserve / cannibalize / defer) fires on the offer->accept path -- Pip hit it at [1:51]-[2:46] and it worked. But #1041 [5:07] already recorded that "the onboarding prompt fires only on the offer->accept path. Other hiring routes complete with no prompt", and fast-track hiring is the named offender here. On those routes a hire lands at reduced output with the player never having made a decision -- exactly the silent-wrongness shape.

So the requirement, as a testable invariant: **every route that produces an employed researcher must surface the onboarding choice window at least once for that hire.** Skipping must be a choice ("[E] Let it wait") the player actively made. Pointers: `godot/scripts/core/hiring_pipeline.gd` (the accept-path window builder at ~:550-604; find the fast-track path that bypasses it), researcher onboarding flags (`laptop_done` etc.), `month_controller.gd` window queue.

## The presentation ask: arrivals come through a door

**[9:39]** "there's probably something about when someone is hired, maybe they come in the door for the first time ... so we have some UI representation of it that's a bit more storyline-based. So this also infers that we then want to spawn in a door, and start thinking of some logic about having people come through it ... Seems like a little pretty easy little pickup."

Concretely for the office sim:
1. A door asset spawned on the office floor (pixellab pipeline; the office already places water cooler / server rack / cat, so the placement pattern exists).
2. New-hire arrival sequence: sprite enters through the door on their start day, then takes a desk -- which doubles as the natural TRIGGER MOMENT for the onboarding window on routes that currently skip it. The two halves of this issue meet at the door.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming the onboarding COSTS or the reserve/cannibalize model change -- the window as built is liked. This is about coverage (all hiring routes) and staging (an in-world arrival beat).
- Not diagnosed: exactly which routes bypass the window today. First task is enumerating them (fast-track confirmed by intent on tape; audit `hiring_pipeline.gd` for others).

Related: #789 (hiring stitch -- the accept-path window this extends), #1041 [5:07] (first record of the coverage gap), #830 (hiring statefulness), #925 (office W3 pre-build, where door logic lives), #924 (cat animations -- sibling office-entity work), #804 (start-date scheduling -- the arrival day this beat would land on).

issues.title: design(research): Research Quality (Rushed/Standard/Thorough) is still a global Plan-screen toggle -- the ruling moved it to research-project level
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frames `f060_376s.jpg`, `f067_411s.jpg`).

## Observation

**[6:49]** "Research quality, rushed, standard, thorough. This doesn't live in this UI, this lives somewhere else. So let's move it out of here. And I think we actually made a decision that this is going to be done at an idea or research project level, rather than as a global level. So let's figure out where this lives inside the more coherent, philosophically aligned version of the game, and then make a plan to move it there."

Frames: the Rushed/Standard/Thorough selector sits at the very top-left of the Plan screen, directly under the attention bar, with its blurb line ("2.0x speed. Erodes research integrity, widens capability overhang.") occupying prime real estate on every planning turn -- for a setting most players will touch once.

## The decision trail (Pip's memory checks out)

- Origin: issue #500 -- built as an org-wide stance. Code: `godot/scripts/ui/research_quality_selector.gd` ("Player picks the org-wide stance"), mounted at `main_ui.gd:245-249` into the plan screen; state in `game_state.gd:234/728-749` (`research_quality_mode`, global multiplier + risk-pool feed).
- `docs/game-design/WORKSHOP_2_BACKLOG.md:520`: "Research Quality Rushed/Standard/Thorough (issue #500, top-left in game) uses literal doom deltas -- dies in the ADR-0015 event-intermediary content pass."
- `docs/game-design/RESEARCH_IDEA_PAPER_PIPELINE_GAP.md` (section 1b): the global mode is called out as the ONLY research direction the player has -- "global, not per-researcher and not per-idea" -- precisely the gap the per-project model (ADR-0011 workstreams; ideas as first-class objects) is meant to fill.

So the ruling Pip remembers is real, recorded in two places, and this selector is the last visible artifact of the pre-ruling model.

## Ask (a plan, not an immediate rip-out)

1. Confirm the target home: quality as a property of a research project/idea (set when work is committed), per RESEARCH_IDEA_PAPER_PIPELINE_GAP + ADR-0011. If that substrate is not built yet, this issue BLOCKS ON it -- do not orphan the mechanic by deleting the only lever first.
2. Interim (cheap, unblocks #1043's layout work): demote the selector out of the Plan screen's prime top-left -- it does not need per-turn prominence even while global.
3. When the per-project model lands: migrate the multiplier + risk feed (`apply_research_quality_risk`) to per-project, delete the global mode, and update `test_research_quality.gd`.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming the mechanic's NUMBERS are wrong (2.0x/0.5x, integrity/overhang feeds) -- only its scope (global) and its screen position.

Related: #500 (origin), #1043 (Plan screen layout -- this selector is part of the clutter it inherits), #986 (ADR-0015 risk_events pass, where the literal-doom-delta content dies), #984 (mechanics deep-dive audit).

issues.title: ui(fanfare): 'Strategic Moves Unlocked' -- the game's biggest milestone beat renders as bare text on black
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frame `f046_307s.jpg`).

## Observation

**[5:05]** "I want a visual, like a poster or a pop-up on the strategic moves unlocked ... This is a cool pop-up thing, but it's also like, well cool, it's just a black little screen, let's make that visually more interesting"

Frame `f046_307s.jpg`: the STRATEGIC MOVES UNLOCKED moment -- "The council of elders has deemed your standing sufficient. High-stakes plays now open to you..." -- renders as centered white text on a dimmed black overlay with a plain Continue button. The copy is doing milestone work; the visuals are doing nothing. This is (with the cold open) the game's biggest single fanfare beat, roughly a year into a run.

Code: `godot/scripts/ui/fanfare_popup.gd` (invoked from `main_ui.gd:1847` with the "STRATEGIC MOVES UNLOCKED" strings). The popup component is generic; it has no art slot.

## Ask

1. Give `fanfare_popup.gd` an optional hero/poster image slot.
2. Commission or promote a poster-style asset for the strategic-moves beat (the endgame poster batch pipeline in #1024 and the gpt-image-1 pipeline are the obvious generators; the in-repo art review flow decides the winner).
3. While in there: the same popup pattern presumably serves other milestone beats -- audit which fanfares exist and which deserve art, so this is one pattern fix, not one screen fix.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming the unlock TIMING or nomenclature is right -- that is #763's scope (month-grain pacing + "align fanfare hero"). This issue is purely the visual treatment of the popup surface. If #763's audit lands first, do the art second; they do not block each other.

Related: #763 (pacing/nomenclature for the same beat), #1024 (poster batch under provisional art rules), #817 (cold-open hero backgrounds -- sibling fanfare surface).

issues.title: Rivals appear for the first time in the month summary, having never been introduced
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frame `f026_206s.jpg`). This was the finding Pip called out hardest.

## Observation

The August month review (frame `f026_206s.jpg`) contains:

```
Rivals this month:
  DeepSafety (safety) -- capabilities flat
  CapabiliCorp (capabilities) -- capabilities flat
  StealthAI (rumored) (balanced) -- capabilities flat
```

**[3:58]** "Now, I've never seen these rivals before, this is the first time this information has appeared in the game"
**[4:02]** "So, we need to think something along the lines of, from a player experience, how do I know that I have rivals? And how has the game told me this? How has the game introduced this concept to me? How do I know what they're doing?"
**[4:18]** "This summary was probably done pre-W3, and so this needs a rework"

Three named organisations, with focus tags and a capability-drift read, appear for the first time in a recap popup -- as if the player already knew who they were. There was no introduction event, no feed beat announcing their existence, no screen where rivals live. (The feed HAS a "Hide rival intel" toggle, visible in `f014_133s.jpg`, so rival intel lines exist as a channel -- but a filter toggle is not an introduction either.)

## Mechanism

`godot/scripts/game_manager.gd:784` `_build_rivals_review_section()` builds the block from "each VISIBLE rival" -- so a visibility model already exists in the data. What does not exist is any moment that takes a rival from invisible to visible IN THE FICTION. Visibility flips somewhere in state; the player experiences it as the summary suddenly assuming context.

## Ask (design, then content)

1. An introduction beat per rival: the first time a rival becomes visible, that is an EVENT -- a feed story or window ("A lab in [city] published a capabilities result...", intel purchase, journalist call), not a bullet in a recap. Pip: "this is like a UI interaction storyline thing, so I think we can crack that out pretty quickly" [4:27].
2. The month-review rivals block should only ever RESTATE rivals the player has met, and say what changed since last month ("capabilities flat" three times at first appearance carries no information).
3. A place rivals live between summaries -- even one line each somewhere inspectable -- so "how do I know what they're doing?" has an answer.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming the rivals sim is wrong -- only its narrative surfacing. The summary text itself Pip liked as a format ("Staff 1, okay, that's cool, rivals this month" [3:55]).
- Not claiming where the intro should fire from -- that is a W3-flavoured design call (event tiers per ADR-0012 look like the natural home).

Related: the rivals-surfacing work from the success-premortem workstream (PRs #725/#726 territory), #825 (event OUTS sweep), #1016 (provenance real infrastructure failures as flavour), #956 (mysterious-stranger delivery pattern -- an existing example of introducing a channel in-fiction).

issues.title: ui(numbers): no format policy -- '$197,207.69' sits beside '82.0', '* 70' and 'money: 3000.0' on one screen
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frame `f024_194s.jpg`).

## Observation

**[3:12]** "and months, years, and cents, and billions"

One top bar at turn 21 (frame `f024_194s.jpg`) shows, left to right:

- `Turn 21 - Tue 1 Aug 2017` -- day-grain date next to a turn counter (the turn/day nomenclature problem, already ruled on in #1041's "Turn is counting days" finding)
- `$197,207.69 (-$238.46)` -- money to the CENT
- `82.0 (-1.0)` and `34.0` -- one-decimal floats for compute/research
- `0`, `* 70` -- bare ints with a sigil
- Attention as `20 *` plus a separate `(0 free, 19 reserved)` readout elsewhere in the same bar

And the hiring tooltip (frame `f015_142s.jpg`) prints `money: 3000.0` -- an internal float where every other money surface writes `$3,000`.

Nothing here is individually wrong; the defect is that there is NO FORMAT POLICY, so precision implies meaning it does not have. Cents on a $197k balance imply cent-level decisions exist (they do not); `82.0` implies fractional compute matters; `3000.0` is a debug string in a player-facing tooltip.

## Ask

One short convention, then a sweep:

- Money: whole dollars with thousands separators (`$197,208`), sign only on deltas. Cents never, unless a mechanic actually trades in cents.
- Resource scalars: ints unless the fraction is meaningful.
- No internal dict-dump formatting (`key: 3000.0`) in any player-facing tooltip.
- Document the ruling in `docs/GLOSSARY.md` or a one-page NUMBER_FORMATS note so future surfaces inherit it.

Likely touch points: the top-bar builder in `godot/scripts/ui/main_ui.gd` (around the `ap_text` block at ~line 1112) and whatever renders window-option cost tooltips.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming which format is right -- that is a 10-minute ruling for Pip. Claiming only that four coexisting formats on one bar is the defect.

Related: #1041 (turn-vs-day counter ruling), #1062 (leaderboard Duration column -- same family: a number displayed without a meaning).

issues.title: ux(hiring): onboard-now window -- tooltip omits the Attention cost (costs dict has money only), prints raw 'money: 3000.0', and Q/W read as the same option
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only; frames in `frames_2026-08-01_09-52-08/`, see `f014_133s.jpg`, `f015_142s.jpg`, `f018_168s.jpg`).

The "Owen Rodriguez said yes" onboarding window (the new hiring-stitch accept prompt) works as a mechanic -- but four presentation defects landed together in one 35-second stretch:

## 1. The tooltip omits the Attention cost and prints a raw float

**[2:11]** "first bug ... this says 3 attention reserved and says it costs 3 money, this is not a really good layout"

Frame `f015_142s.jpg`: hovering `[Q] Set them up now (3 Att from reserve) ($3,000)` shows a tooltip reading `Costs: money: 3000.0`. Mechanism, verified in code: `godot/scripts/core/hiring_pipeline.gd:597` builds the option as `"costs": {"money": money}` -- the Attention cost lives only in the label TEXT, not in the structured costs dict, so whatever renders the costs tooltip can only ever show money. The tooltip also renders the internal key and float verbatim (`money: 3000.0`) instead of `$3,000`.

The tooltip additionally OCCLUDES the [W] option's label while hovering [Q] (visible in the frame), hiding exactly the text that distinguishes the two options.

## 2. Q and W read as the same option

**[2:20]** "the Q option is not a good layout, the W option is not a good layout"

The two labels are `[Q] Set them up now (3 Att from reserve) ($3,000)` and `[W] Set them up now (3 Att, pull from planned work) ($3,000)` -- identical first four words, identical price, the load-bearing difference buried mid-parenthesis. The reserve-vs-cannibalize choice is the crisp teaching moment of the window system (per `hiring_pipeline.gd:550` comment) and the layout hides it.

## 3. An unpayable option is offered, then errors after the click

**[2:34]** "Can I pull from planned work ... I can't pull from planned work, whatever"

Frame `f018_168s.jpg`: after choosing [W], an error line appears under the options: `[!] Insufficient capacity to handle by cannibalizing -- pick another option.` The message source is `godot/scripts/core/window_resolver.gd:91`; the option existed but could not be paid (`month_controller.gd:298` documents exactly this state). The window should know at render time that cannibalize cannot be paid (no free capacity, no WIP at turn 3) and show the option disabled with the reason, instead of letting the player pick it and bounce.

## 4. "Cannibalizing" is internal vocabulary leaking to the player

**[2:46]** "Insufficient capacity to handle by cannibalizing, okay"

`handle_reserve` / `handle_cannibalize` are the ENGINE's verb names (`window_resolver.gd:6`). "Cannibalizing" in a player-facing error, with no prior introduction of the term, reads as jargon. The player-facing copy should say what it means: "not enough unplanned capacity -- you would have to cancel planned work, and there is none to cancel".

## Ask

- Put the Attention cost into the costs dict (or teach the tooltip renderer to read both), and format money as money.
- Restructure the two set-up-now options so the SOURCE is the visible difference (e.g. one action, source picker).
- Disable-with-reason unpayable options at render time.
- Copy pass on the cannibalize failure text.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming the mechanic is wrong -- reserve-vs-cannibalize as an explicit choice is working as designed and Pip used it. This is presentation.

Related: #789 (the hiring stitch that built this window), #1041 (previous playtest hiring findings), #830 (hiring statefulness), #855 (Attention readout in event-dialog corner).

issues.title: bug(window): minimising v0.13.2 does not minimise -- window left in a wrong state until re-maximised (first run after #1079)
issues.body:
From the recorded playtest of the freshly built v0.13.2, 2026-08-01 09:52 (`art_generated/audiodump/2026-08-01_09-52-08.transcript.md`, local-only/gitignored; frames in `frames_2026-08-01_09-52-08/`).

## Observation

**[1:02]** "I'm going to minimise the screen, and then, that's interesting, well, I mean, that's probably not expected behaviour"
**[1:16]** "Okay, now I'm going to maximise it, so, that one was a bit of an interesting fix"

Frame `f005_64s.jpg` (~2s after the minimise attempt) shows the game still occupying the full screen -- the main menu fully rendered, cursor parked at the top-right where the window buttons live. Whatever "minimise" did, the window did not go to the taskbar; Pip had to re-maximise to get back to a good state (`f006_78s.jpg` looks normal again). Between f004 (before) and f005 (during), the menu renders at a visibly different scale, consistent with the window having restored to a different size/mode rather than minimising.

## Why this is flagged as a possible #1079 interaction

This is the FIRST run of a build containing PR #1079, which rewrote the corner build badge (`godot/scripts/ui/dev_build_badge.gd`) and newly connects `get_viewport().size_changed` to a refit callback that runs on every window resize -- minimise included. Reading the diff: the callback only recomputes the badge panel's own offsets, so a mechanism where it blocks or reverses a window minimise is not apparent. The badge itself renders correctly in every frame.

**Not diagnosed.** The recording shows the symptom but not the cause. Alternative candidate: engine/window-mode behaviour -- the game has no window mode options at all (#820), and how the project handles minimise/restore under whatever mode the release build launches in has never been specified.

Secondary observation from the same frames: the version label appears TWICE on the main menu -- the #1079 quiet corner badge top-right AND a second `v0.13.2` bottom-right (the welcome screen's own stamped label). One of them is redundant now.

## Ask

1. 30-second repro on the v0.13.2 release artifact: maximise, minimise, watch what happens. If it reproduces, capture window mode + what state the window lands in.
2. If it is the badge's `size_changed` handling, fix there; if it is window-mode handling, fold into #820's scope.
3. Decide which of the two version labels survives.

## Not claimed

- Not claiming #1079 caused it -- the diff gives no mechanism for it. Flagged because it is the only window-adjacent change in this build.
- Not claiming the game was unusable -- re-maximising recovered it immediately.

Related: #1079 (badge rewrite), #820 (window mode options), #1041 (previous playtest's findings).

issues.title: The difficulty lock (#1058) is enforced at a UI screen, not where difficulty is consumed -- Settings can still write Easy/Hard
issues.body:
Found 2026-08-01 while reviewing the settings menu. **Third instance this week of the same structural mistake**, and this one is live on the league board.

## The guarantee we believe we have

#1058, merged on league day, locked difficulty to Standard so that every entry on the board is comparable. The board key contains no difficulty field, so an Easy run and a Hard run would otherwise land on one board silently incomparable.

## Why the guarantee does not hold

The lock lives in **`godot/scripts/ui/pregame_setup.gd:62`**:

```gdscript
GameConfig.difficulty = 1  # Standard
difficulty_option.selected = 1
difficulty_option.disabled = true
```

That is one UI screen. But difficulty is **consumed** somewhere else entirely -- `GameManager.start_new_game()` calls `_apply_difficulty_settings()` (`game_manager.gd:89`, defined at `:968`), which reads `GameConfig.difficulty` and scales the **monthly Attention grant** from the Balance surface. That is a real balance lever, not cosmetic.

Meanwhile the **Settings menu writes difficulty freely**, with no lock at all:

```gdscript
# godot/scripts/ui/settings_menu.gd:163
func _on_difficulty_changed(index: int):
    GameConfig.set_setting("difficulty", index, false)
```

`GameConfig.difficulty` is persisted to `config.cfg`, so it survives a restart.

**And `pregame_setup` is one of at least six routes into `main.tscn`:**

```
cold_open_sequence.gd:608     -> main.tscn
config_confirmation.gd:93     -> main.tscn   <-- the ONLY locked path (follows pregame_setup)
leaderboard_screen.gd:707     -> main.tscn
settings_menu.gd:344          -> main.tscn
welcome_screen.gd:175         -> main.tscn
```

So the guarantee "every board entry is a Standard run" is enforced by **one screen out of several**, on a value read at a completely different point in the lifecycle.

## What is NOT claimed

I have **not** confirmed that any specific alternate route actually reaches `start_new_game()` with a settings-written difficulty and posts a ranked score. Several of those routes may resume rather than start, and `start_new_game()` has a `force` self-guard. **The defect asserted here is structural**: the invariant is not enforced where the value is consumed, so whether it currently holds is an accident of routing rather than a property of the design. That is exactly the kind of thing that is true until someone adds a nav edge.

## The pattern, because it is the third time in seven days

| When | Fix | Where it was enforced | What was missed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 07-31 11:14 | #1058 difficulty | a UI screen | the other entry points, and Settings |
| 07-31 16:15 | #1060 scenario | `GameConfig.is_ranked_run()` -- **the consumption point** | nothing so far |
| 08-01 | this | -- | -- |

**#1060 is the model and #1058 is the anti-pattern.** #1060 put a named accessor at the single place board writes happen, precisely so a future caller could not forget it. #1058 set a variable on one screen and trusted the routing.

## Fix

Enforce at consumption, not at presentation. Either:

1. **`_apply_difficulty_settings()` forces Standard while the league lock is in effect**, ignoring `GameConfig.difficulty` entirely -- smallest, and mirrors #1060's shape; or
2. **A `GameConfig.effective_difficulty()` accessor** that returns the locked value, with every consumer routed through it and the raw field made private-by-convention; or
3. **Route a non-Standard difficulty through `is_ranked_run()`** so such runs stay playable but unranked -- consistent with the scenario ruling, and arguably the most honest answer once the lock is lifted.

Also fix regardless: the Settings dropdown should be disabled with the same tooltip `pregame_setup` uses, rather than silently writing a value the game may or may not honour.

## Related

- **#1058** difficulty lock, **#1060** scenario gating (the model to copy)
- **#1027** the failure family; `docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md`, section "the instance-versus-class problem is the expensive one"
- Website **#191** froze the submission surface, so option 1 or 2 is preferable to anything that changes what is submitted

issues.title: The GDScript syntax gate does not compile-check -- a hard parse error passed it clean
issues.body:
Found 2026-08-01 as an incidental during PR #1081, and it is a weakness in a guard rather than in game code.

## What happened

`var at := anchor.get_index()` on an untyped var is a **hard parse error** in Godot 4. It was written, and `scripts/run_godot_tests.py`'s GDScript syntax check **passed it clean**.

The error did not surface as a syntax failure. It surfaced as **16 unrelated UI tests failing** with:

```
Nonexistent function 'new' in base 'GDScript'
```

-- which is what you get downstream when a script fails to parse and its class object never materialises. Anyone reading that output would start debugging the sixteen tests, not the one line that broke them.

## The mechanism

The gate reports `[PASS] GDScript syntax check passed!` without ever asking the engine to compile the scripts. `godot --check-only --script <path>` does perform a real parse; whatever the gate currently runs does not.

So the check's name promises a property it does not verify. This is the failure family tracked in **#1027**: a proxy for truth (the gate says syntax is fine) silently detached from the truth (the script does not parse), and nothing was watching the join. It is the same shape as the CI gate that reported green while running zero tests (#640) -- and #640 is the direct precedent for why this matters here specifically.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than later

1. **It corrupts diagnosis, not just coverage.** A parse error that presents as sixteen unrelated failures sends the reader to the wrong place. That cost is paid every time it happens, by whoever is unlucky.
2. **The failure is silent in the direction that matters.** It cannot produce a false alarm, only a false all-clear.
3. **Agent-authored changes make it more likely.** Several lanes now write GDScript in parallel worktrees and lean on the fast gate as their proof of correctness. A gate that cannot see a parse error is exactly the wrong gate to lean on.

## Fix

Make the gate actually compile. `godot --headless --check-only --script <path>` per changed `.gd` file, or the equivalent whole-tree invocation, with a non-zero exit failing the gate.

**Verify the fix by proving it fails:** reintroduce `var at := anchor.get_index()` in a scratch file and confirm the gate goes red. A guard that has never been observed failing has not been tested -- that is the #640 lesson, and it should be applied to its own successor.

## Related

- **#640** -- CI reported green while running zero tests. Same class, same repo, already fixed once.
- **#1027** -- the phase-transition issue tracking this failure family.
- **PR #1081** -- where this surfaced.
- `docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md` -- eleven instances of the same shape in one afternoon.

issues.title: Postmortem contribution from pdoom1-website: the league opened, and the site hid it for 90 minutes
issues.body:
Contributed from the **pdoom1-website** side for the 2026-08-01 postmortem, covering
2026-07-29 → 08-01. Written to be useful rather than flattering; the mistakes section is
the longest one on purpose.

**Numbers, measured not recalled:** 30 PRs merged, 114 commits to `main`, 8 issues closed
with evidence, 10 PRs still open (all deliberate), 42 issues open.

---

# 1. The headline: the league opened, and the website hid it for ~90 minutes

**What happened.** The seed was blessed at ~18:45 AEST Friday, rolling from
`weekly-2026-w30` to `weekly-2026-w31`. pdoom1.com kept serving the **previous** board
until 18:47. During that window three real players scored and could not see themselves.

**Nothing was lost.** Every score was in the API the whole time. But the site rendered as
*"nobody is playing"* — which is precisely the misdiagnosis the board-honesty subsystem was
built to prevent, arriving through the one door it did not watch.

**Root cause, and it is structural rather than careless.** `check-board-liveness.py`
derives its probe set instead of hardcoding it — deliberately, and that is the right
instinct. But it derives candidate *seeds* only from files that have **already seen one**:
the preserved captures, `weekly/current.json`, `leaderboard.json`, `published-board.json`.
A freshly drawn seed appears in none of them.

So on the first run after the roll it probed **108 boards** and reported:

```
OK: deployed board (weekly-2026-w30, L3) holds 3 entries.
```

Green. Confident. Wrong.

**The asymmetry is the lesson.** A ladder epoch is a *counter*, so a `+2` forward window
finds a bump automatically (it probed `L1..L14` that night). **A seed is a drawn string**,
so no equivalent lookahead is possible — and the ceremony is exactly the moment a new one
appears. Every guard in this system was built to distrust absence; this one trusted its own
input list, and that list could not contain the answer.

**Fixed**, verified live end-to-end, and filed as pdoom1-website#229. The durable fix reads
the blessed seed from `ladder-epochs.json` — closing the loop between the ledger entry the
ceremony *already requires* and the monitor, so the paperwork becomes the mechanism. After
that, from the release artifact, since the game already pins it at
`GameConfig.FEATURED_SEED_OVERRIDE`.

**Cross-repo note worth acting on:** that const is the authoritative answer and it is
reachable — `git grep FEATURED_SEED_OVERRIDE v0.13.2 -- godot/` is how the seed was
ultimately confirmed. If a release asset carried it, the website would need no human step at
all. That is a small game-side change with a disproportionate payoff.

---

# 2. What the week actually bought

Stated because the postmortem should weigh cost against benefit, and the benefit is
otherwise invisible — it consists of things that did *not* happen.

**Found and fixed, all pre-existing and all silent:**

- **A live stored-XSS hole on the leaderboard.** The score API is unauthenticated and
  validates nothing, so one crafted POST ran script for every visitor. It had never fired
  only because the shipped client generates lab names from a fixed table — which constrains
  the client, not an attacker with `curl`. Found while chasing an unrelated feature request.
- **A deploy trap.** Fourteen workflows commit files under `public/`; **one** could make the
  site update. A push made with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not trigger another
  workflow, so everything else landed in git and stopped. The RSS feed's own header says
  *"a feed that silently stops updating is worse than no feed"* — and it had been.
- **`status.json` frozen since 2026-07-17**, advertising **v0.11.0** on the homepage beside
  a derived v0.13.1. A visitor saw two answers eight months apart, on the day we were about
  to invite people. One missing `git add` line.
- **A CI guard that had never once passed** since the day it shipped, blocking unrelated PRs
  *and* freezing a page that told readers the league resets on Monday when the config said
  Friday.
- **A page that a missing WebGL context could kill entirely** — decoration taking the content
  down with it, on a top-level nav page.
- **A test fixture rotting for three releases**, red the whole time, inside the suite the
  docs tell you to run before every PR.
- **Invented numbers presented as measurements**: `baseline_doom_percent: 23` and
  `strategic_possibilities: 10000` hardcoded in three places and rendered under confident
  labels, with the homepage announcing *"This week's baseline doom percentage"* for a weekly
  calculation that has never run.
- **75 academics' institutional email addresses** served from 44 pages.
- **"Free and open source"** across the site, when the licence says *"All rights reserved …
  No license is granted to redistribute."*

**Built, so the next league is cheaper:** a read-only board publisher that refuses rather
than guesses; forced-failure tests for every one of its refusal paths; an escaping guard
that enforces the *class* rather than a field list; a control-character check; a surface
register; a league cycle handbook; and print-first paper artifacts for the ceremony.

---

# 3. Mistakes — mine, in full

The longest section because it should be.

**3.1 I dismissed a real finding by checking the wrong artifact.** An audit reported
`status.json` was serving v0.11.0. I checked, saw v0.13.1, and told Pip the finding was
stale. I had read my **working tree**, which I had just regenerated — the committed and
deployed file said v0.11.0 the whole time. **Cost: ~7 more hours of a wrong version on the
homepage, on announcement day.** I had written the `[verified]` vs `[reported]` discipline
into our own register the night before, and then failed it.

**3.2 I bundled too much into one command during an incident.** At ~18:20 Friday, with the
board wrong, I ran publish + commit + push as one chain. It hit a 2-minute timeout, the
commit never completed, and I reported the state as unknown. **The outage ran ~25 minutes
longer than it needed to.** Rule taken: *under time pressure, one action per command.*

**3.3 I shipped an incomplete fix and a test that could not catch it.** The first escaping
pass closed six fields and left thirteen open — `entry_uuid`, `final_money` and friends,
which *look* numeric but where `|| 0` does not coerce a string and `toLocaleString()` is the
identity function. Worse, the test I wrote **named six fields**, so it passed while thirteen
were open. Fixed by enforcing the class, not a list. **A list that must be remembered is a
list that goes stale.**

**3.4 The guard I wrote could never run on the machine it was written for.** `core.autocrlf`
means a Windows checkout is CRLF; my extractor anchored on `;\n`. It failed on the only
platform the docs tell you to run it on, while passing in a CI that did not run it either.
It only ever passed for me because I had written the file from Python with LF preserved.

**3.5 Three heredoc escape-manglings in one day**, in a repo whose CLAUDE.md documents that
exact trap twice and says to use the editing tools. One broke `main`. **One was silent** — a
raw `0x08` byte where a word boundary was intended, inside an otherwise valid regex, so the
guard matched nothing and reported *"found 0 interpolations to check"* and **passed**. That
silent one is why a control-character check now exists.

**3.6 Three branches pushed without opening a PR.** The second caused work to be built on
the wrong base, silently removing a stamp from 1,194 pages before I caught it. The third
meant Pip ran a command that did not exist on his branch.

**3.7 I broke `main` three times inside 90 minutes**, all guard misfires rather than product
defects. Mean time to green under 15 minutes each — *because the failures were loud*. That
part worked.

**3.8 I patched one guard twice in one morning without stepping back.** The seed-leak rule
greps a whole directory, so it fired on a test fixture, then on a mirror of issue text. Each
false positive is indistinguishable from a real leak until a human reads it. I fixed the
instances and only afterwards named the shape: the durable fix is an allowlist of files that
can actually *feed* a seed.

---

# 4. Process observations, offered as data

**4.1 The clock.** At session open the machine read **~3.5 hours ahead** of the stated time.
Every "we have ages" judgement before that was made against a wrong clock, including one
that assumed Gate 4's window was open when it had closed. *Recommendation: stamp the machine
clock at session open, before planning anything against it.* Cheapest fix in this document.

**4.2 The freeze was overridden, not observed.** A 13:00 reader-facing freeze was set at
07:34; the last reader-facing merge was 15:01. Both breaches were deliberate — fixes to
information that was live and wrong on the page about to be advertised. **That is a freeze
being applied correctly, not a failure of discipline.** But the record should say
"overridden," and a freeze that cannot be broken for a live lie is the wrong rule.

**4.3 Red that means nothing trains you to ignore red.** Pip's own observation this week, and
the most useful thing either of us said: he had trained himself to ignore red tests because
*the redness never forced him to slow down*. That is correct Bayesian housekeeping, not
carelessness — the defect was in the signal. The rule taken: **a check must be
blocking-and-true or advisory-and-labelled, never red-but-tolerated.** Pip then improved it
by pointing out a legitimate third state from his data-quality practice: **a large finite
population being burned down against a trend**. A big number is fine; a number with no owner
and no trajectory is not.

Live instances found afterwards, all manufacturing noise: an invalid workflow file reddening
**every push on every branch**; rolling alert issues with **no close path**, so they stay
open even when the condition clears; and a data-validation alert gating on whole-job failure,
so a `git push` race posts *"Still failing"* when validation actually reported `0 fail`.

**4.4 Guards that pass vacuously.** `check-platform-claims.py` returns **before scanning a
single page** when all platforms are true. Combined with a second workflow that deletes the
field it reads, that gate has **two independent ways of passing without checking**. Eight
guards in the repo have only ever been observed passing, with nothing proving they *can*
fail.

**4.5 Audit findings are leads, not facts.** Five parallel audits produced excellent
material. **Two confident, well-argued findings with real line numbers did not survive
checking.** Both are recorded in the register at §4.9 rather than quietly dropped, because a
register that hides its own errors is the thing it exists to prevent.

---

# 5. On "spread myself out too sideways"

Pip raised this and I want to argue with it, carefully.

**The parallel work is why Friday's outage was 90 minutes rather than the weekend.** The
monitor that eventually caught the wrong board, the publisher that fixed it in one command,
and the honesty layer that would have told visitors "we cannot confirm this board" were all
built in the preceding 48 hours. Without them, the site would have served a stale board with
no mechanism to notice.

**And the cost was real.** Three `main`-red incidents, an incomplete escaping fix, a test
that could not run, and a 7-hour wrong version on the homepage all happened *because* a lot
was moving at once.

**So both are true, and the postmortem should say both** rather than filing it under "should
have focused." The sharper question is not *how much* was in flight but **how much of it
needed Pip**. The work that went badly was disproportionately the work that needed a human
decision mid-flight. The work that went well was the work that could be verified against
evidence without one.

*If there is one structural lesson: batch the decisions, not the work.*

---

# 6. What would make the next league materially cheaper

Ordered by payoff, not effort.

1. **Emit the featured seed as a release artifact** (game side). Removes the human step that
   caused the outage entirely. Small change, disproportionate payoff.
2. **Give the probe a `seed-unconfirmed` verdict.** Right now, after a roll it can only say
   `OK` or `orphaned`. It had no way to express *"I may not have asked about the right
   board"* — which was the true state. Absence of evidence must be unknown, never a clean
   bill of health.
3. **Kill the manufactured reds** — the invalid workflow file, the close-paths on rolling
   alerts, the push-race alert gate. Each is minutes of work and each is currently teaching
   everyone to ignore a channel.
4. **Baseline doom is available and would be genuinely good copy.** The game's baseline
   simulator is real and works; run with no player actions it reaches 100% doom on roughly
   **3 September 2018**. Eight years ago, obviously wrong, unmistakably a game statistic
   rather than a forecast — and far better than the invented 23% it replaces. It wants an
   emit and a re-run on L3.
5. **Continuity, which is cheap and nobody owns.** No registrar, renewal date or DNS record
   exists in version control for pdoom1.com; the cross-repo server index is explicitly
   local-only; there are zero runbook or continuity files in either repo. **$0 and about two
   hours.**
6. **The privacy gap.** The live privacy page covers *website* analytics only, but the game
   phones home by default. A player reading pdoom1.com/privacy would not learn that.
   Independent of Steam, and a prime-directive issue.

---

# 7. The one thing I would carry forward above all others

Every defect found this week shared a property, and it was **not** carelessness. Each one
produced *no signal a busy person could act on*. The XSS looked like working code. The deploy
trap looked like a successful workflow run. The frozen version looked like fresh data. The
rotting test looked like a red you had learned to scroll past. The wrong board reported
`OK`.

**The work that pays is not finding bugs. It is making the system capable of telling you
when it is wrong** — and then making sure the telling costs you something to ignore.
